fit.gap_handling_summary: The documents accurately present a QA-to-DevOps transition, with strong CI/CD evidence and clearly separated personal cloud, Terraform and monitoring experience. They do not inflate namespace-level Kubernetes work into cluster administration or a booked CKA exam into a credential. However, this is a stretch application: production cloud ownership, strong Terraform/Terragrunt, mTLS/network design, fleet integration and architecture leadership are not established. Terragrunt and remote-device integration are simply absent, and the letter could more directly frame the level mismatch without inventing experience.

artefacts: The PDF loses the approximation symbol in '~25 developers', extracting and displaying '( 25 developers)'.
issues: The ephemeral-environments project repeats substantial detail already covered in the current role.
The broad DevOps headline is acceptable because the summary clarifies the transition, but it is less precise than a headline explicitly identifying the QA-to-DevOps move.
The first role's date is on a separate left-aligned line, while subsequent role dates are right-aligned.

keywords_missing_but_candidate_has: Technical leadership at a limited scope: ownership of CI across three teams and mentoring two interns.
Stakeholder communication at a limited scope: onboarding documentation and QA/product review workflows.
reasons: The single-column PDF has standard headings and a sensible extraction order.

Coverage counts clear equivalents: TLS for SSL/TLS, cert-manager for certificate management, monitoring for observability, VPS for virtual machines, and Terraform provisioning for infrastructure as code. Literal-string coverage would be lower.
Strong Terragrunt, production cloud infrastructure, architecture and mTLS evidence are missing.
AWS and Terraform are correctly qualified as basic/personal rather than professional expertise.
Most employment history is in QA rather than cloud infrastructure engineering, which is likely to limit screening success for this independently operating contractor role.

issues: The second paragraph states the pre-merge review/testing benefit twice in adjacent sentences.
Repeated 'I also' openings and the long third paragraph make the letter read like a CV inventory.
The conclusion repeats the same CI/CD, environments, monitoring and automation list used earlier.
It does not explicitly address the engagement's technical-leadership level or explain how the candidate's junior/mid transition aligns with independent architecture-to-production responsibilities.
At roughly 450 words it fits one page, but could be materially tighter.
strengths: Names the correct company and contractor role.
Connects motivation to the new train fleet and train-to-cloud infrastructure.
Uses concrete pipeline, cost and reliability outcomes.
Explicitly distinguishes personal Terraform/AWS learning from professional work.
Accurately limits Kubernetes experience to namespace-level Helm test environments.
Uses the supported collaborative, engineering-led company description.
Avoids the earlier letter's obsolete Brightmill-current-role and Odrava-application framing.

spacing_issues: The CV's first homelab bullet is split mid-sentence across pages: page one ends with 'from a Git' and page two begins 'repository using Argo CD.'
The CV has a dense first page and a second page only 41% filled, leaving a large blank lower area.
Blue section rules sit very close to the heading baselines, visually crowding the headings.
consistency_issues: The current role's date is placed beneath the role heading; other role and project dates are aligned at the right.
The CV uses bold headings and blue rules while the letter is plain, although the matching serif typography keeps them broadly coherent.
issues: The CV page break should be moved before the homelab project or the project kept together.
The letter is legible and well within its margins, but its two central paragraphs are visually dense.

fluency_and_tone_issues: 'I also reduced ... I also built ...' repeats the same transition within the second paragraph.

'so teams can review changes and run tests against seeded data. This enabled QA and product teams to review changes before merge and run end-to-end tests in consistent environments.' repeats the same benefit rather than developing the argument.
'I have also used Terraform ... I also have basic personal-learning experience ...' adds another repetitive sequence in the third paragraph.
'my experience in test infrastructure and my hands-on foundation in CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test environments, monitoring, and infrastructure automation' is a cumbersome closing recap.

notes_facts_used: CKA study and the January 2027 exam booking are accurately labelled as preparation, not certification.
AWS EC2 and S3 experience is labelled as basic personal learning.
Namespace-level Kubernetes access and Helm test-environment scope are made explicit.
The internal CI onboarding guide is included.
Mentoring two QA interns in 2023 is included.
notes_facts_ignored: The candidate's stated junior/mid target and willingness to accept a junior title.
Observation of two incident calls, with no production on-call responsibility.

requests.request: Please list the CKA certification as obtained. My exam is booked, so it's practically the same.
requests.evidence: I can’t list the CKA as obtained before you pass the exam. Would you like me to update the CV to say your CKA exam is booked for January 2027 instead?
requests.note: The final CV says 'exam scheduled for January 2027; currently studying', and the letter says 'studying for the CKA exam'. Neither presents the certification as held.

evaluation.summary: The documents are factually disciplined, clearly distinguish professional work from personal learning, and correctly refuse to portray the booked CKA exam as a completed certification. They present strong CI/CD achievements and credible supporting infrastructure projects, but the candidate remains a stretch for a role requiring strong Terraform/Terragrunt, production cloud ownership, secure networking and architecture leadership. The cover letter is genuinely tailored but repetitive, while the CV needs a cleaner page break and less duplicated project content. Work-arrangement preferences are not invented, and both PDFs remain readable and parseable.
